newsitem.title: FRANCE: Roussel Uclaf withdraws some OPOS products.
newsitem.headline: Roussel Uclaf withdraws some OPOS products.

text.p: Roussel Uclaf said it had decided after meetings with the FDA to voluntary withdraw the Abbreviated Antibiotic Drug Applications (AADA's) for bulk drugs, held by its OPOS Italian unit, from the U.S. market.
The products concerned are Cefaclor, Minocycline and Clindamycine Phosphate.
Roussel Uclaf is majority-owned by Hoechst AG of Germany.
Biochimica OPOS is an Italian company specialised in the production and sales to third parties of a number of antibiotic active ingredients in the form of bulk substance.

Roussel Uclaf, which is 100 percent owner of Biochimica OPOS since 1993, said it had recently informed the FDA of "some documentation and record keeping issues in the chemical production process of said subsidiary."

"Since the issues identified have not shown any concern regarding the quality of the products, which undergo necessary testing at OPOS as well as at customers who produce finished drug products, the recall does not affect in process products or finished products in the field," it said in a statement.

It said new applications for these bulk products would be filed in the shortest possible time, in cooperation with the FDA, in order to resume sales of these bulk products in the U.S. as soon as possible.
Bulk sales of the three products in the first nine months of 1996 amounted around $60 million.
Francois Gros, spokesman for the group, said the voluntary recall was for the U.S. only because there was only some incompleteness in OPOS FDA's documents.
"It's purely an adminstrative issue, there is no quality problem," Gros said, adding it could take some three months before the new FDA registration could be completed.
He said the description of the production process provided by OPOS was not as detailed as the FDA requires. "Perhaps out of fear the competition could steal the details, I don't know," he said.
He said the costs of the recall would be "several tens of millions of dollars" in lost sales and other costs.
He said buyers of the product were not obliged to return their batches but could opt to do so and Roussel Uclaf would then take the product back.
